title: Nominal sentences
objectives: Recognize sentences without a written verb 'to be'
content: Egyptian can make complete sentences by placing nominal elements together without an explicit equivalent of English 'is'. The particle pw is important in several nominal sentence patterns. Analyze predicate type before translating mechanically.

examples.english: He/it is a scribe / It is a scribe

quiz.q: Must every Egyptian nominal sentence contain a verb meaning 'to be'?

title: Adjectival sentences
content: An adjective can function as the predicate of a sentence. Word order and agreement help distinguish 'the good house' from 'the house is good'. Context is decisive.

examples.english: the house is good (predicative pattern, context dependent)

quiz.q: Can nfr function as a predicate rather than merely modifying a noun?

title: Adverbial and existential sentences
content: Egyptian commonly predicates a prepositional phrase or adverbial expression. Existential and circumstantial particles/constructions play major roles. These patterns are central to translating natural prose.

examples.english: he is in the house (common pedagogical analysis)

quiz.q: In 'jw.f m pr', what supplies the location?

title: Basic verbal word order
content: Many Middle Egyptian verbal clauses show verb–subject–object order, although Egyptian syntax has many constructions that do not fit one simple template. A suffix pronoun may directly encode the subject after the verb form.

examples.english: he hears the speech / he listens to the words (form depends on context)

title: The sḏm.f family
objectives: Avoid assigning one English tense automatically
content: Egyptologists use the model verb sḏm 'hear' to label verbal forms. sḏm.f literally names a form where the verb is followed by a suffix subject. Its temporal/aspectual translation depends heavily on syntactic environment and scholarly analysis, so it should not be equated mechanically with one English tense.

examples.english: he hears / may hear / contextual verbal form

quiz.q: Does sḏm.f always equal the English simple present?

title: The sḏm.n.f construction
content: A common verbal construction traditionally written sḏm.n.f contains the verb, n, and suffix subject. It is often associated with completed events in many contexts, but its full grammatical interpretation is richer than a single past-tense label.

quiz.q: Which element appears between the verb and suffix pronoun in sḏm.n.f?

title: The stative
content: The stative (also called old perfective in older scholarship) describes a state, often resulting from an action. Its endings encode person/number and it behaves differently from the suffix-conjugation forms.

examples.english: state/result pattern; exact form taught with attested examples

quiz.q: Is the stative simply another spelling of sḏm.n.f?

title: Negation
content: Egyptian uses several negative particles and negative constructions. n and nn are especially important, but the correct negative depends on clause type and verbal construction. Do not insert one universal 'not' before every sentence.

quiz.q: Does Middle Egyptian have only one universal negative construction?
